brief.situation: 10:00 on a stroke unit. You are the physical therapist on the wound team, consulted for Mrs. Hughes, 79, on day 2 after a left hemisphere stroke. She is incontinent of urine, eats less than half her meals and slides down the bed.
handover: The nurse says her right heel 'looks bruised'.

Hospital policy: Braden 12 or less is high risk; the wound team recommends the support surface, offloading and nutrition consult, and tells the nurse and provider the same shift; suspected deep tissue injury is offloaded at once.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

scoring.modelReasoning: Assess pressure injury risk with the Braden scale's six areas (sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, friction and shear) plus hydration and cognition. Mrs. Hughes scores 11, high risk. Purple-maroon, intact, non-blanching skin over the heel is a suspected deep tissue pressure injury: float the heels at once, use a pressure-redistributing surface, plan repositioning around her risk factors, address nutrition, and never massage it.

dtiQ.ask: While the surface comes: how is a suspected deep tissue injury handled?

choices.label: Cover it and leave it loaded

dtiQ.explain: A deep tissue pressure injury is persistent non-blanchable deep red, maroon or purple discoloration that may evolve rapidly to reveal the actual extent of tissue injury, so it is protected from further pressure.
